prompt.context: You are out to dinner with a colleague at Sam's Sushi, a Michelin-starred sushi restaurant in Wichita, Kansas. Sam's rose to prominence due to its unerring commitment to both quality and simplicity — Sam prides himself on only serving two items: sushi and sake. After a few sushi rolls and more glasses of sake than you care to count, your colleague asks you how much you think the restaurant is worth and whether or not buying it would be a good investment.
prompt.question: How would you go about determining the value of the restaurant?

clarifying_info.a: No, it is only one restaurant.

clarifying_info.q: What days is the restaurant open?
clarifying_info.a: Sam's is closed on Mondays; it operates the rest of the week.

exhibits.title: Daily Sales
exhibits.shows: A table of daily sales figures broken down by day-of-week category (Fridays and Saturdays vs. Rest of Week) and season (Spring/Summer vs. Fall/Winter). Some cells show dollar amounts and others show relative percentages.

data.rest_of_week_spring_summer: 16.667% of Friday and Saturday (Spring and Summer)
data.friday_saturday_fall_winter: 3/4 of Spring and Summer (Fridays and Saturdays)
data.rest_of_week_fall_winter: 85% of Spring and Summer (Rest of Week)

framework: Revenue – Cost framework to determine annual cash flows
Revenue drivers: number of items (sushi + sake) sold and their prices; can be estimated by product, by customer, or by timeframe
Cost structure: Fixed costs (rent, maintenance, insurance, labor, license fees) and Variable costs (COGS: rice, fish, soy sauce, wasabi, sake)
Valuation: Present value of future cash flows using a perpetuity formula given stable long-run growth

questions.prompt: How would you estimate Sam's average revenues? What factors might cause variation in revenues?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify at least three estimation approaches: (1) by product — number of rolls/sake sold times average price; (2) by customer — customers per day times average spend; (3) by timeframe — average daily sales times operating days per year. Variation factors include day of week (Fri/Sat busier) and seasonality (lighter meals preferred in warmer months).

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate Sam's annual revenue.
questions.guidance: Candidate should work through all four cells of the table, account for 25 weeks of Spring/Summer and 25 weeks of Fall/Winter (50 operating weeks per year), and that the restaurant is closed Mondays (so 4 non-Fri/Sat weekdays per week). The 16.667% figure is 1/6.

math.setup: Annual revenue = (Fri/Sat Spring/Summer) + (Weekday Spring/Summer) + (Fri/Sat Fall/Winter) + (Weekday Fall/Winter)

questions.prompt: Given the cost structure and growth rates below, calculate annual cash flows and the value of the restaurant. [Variable costs: 20% of total revenue; Fixed costs: $120,000/year; Tax rate: 40%; Discount rate: 13%; Annual growth rate of cash flows: 3%]
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total costs, subtract from revenue for EBIT, apply taxes to get after-tax cash flow, then apply the growing perpetuity formula (CF / (r - g)).

math.setup: After-tax cash flow = (Revenue - Fixed Costs - Variable Costs) * (1 - Tax Rate); Value = After-tax CF / (Discount Rate - Growth Rate)
math.answer: Annual after-tax cash flow of ~$200,400; restaurant value of ~$2M

brainstorming.prompt: What factors might cause variation in Sam's revenues?

categories.name: Day of week
ideas: Fridays and Saturdays generate higher traffic
Weekday demand is lower; restaurant is closed Mondays

categories.name: Seasonality
ideas: Spring and Summer drive higher sales (lighter meals preferred)
Fall and Winter see reduced demand

categories.name: Special events
ideas: Holidays or local events can spike traffic
Valentine's Day, New Year's Eve as peak nights

categories.name: Competitive environment
ideas: Limited high-end sushi competition in Wichita supports pricing power

categories.name: Menu/price changes
ideas: Sake price increases or premium sushi offerings
Limited menu (2 items) reduces complexity but caps upsell

recommendation: Sam's Sushi generates approximately $200K in annual after-tax cash flow and is valued at approximately $2M using a growing perpetuity model
At $2M for a single-location restaurant in a small market, the valuation is high but supportable given the Michelin-star reputation, healthy margins, and low overhead
risks: Concentration risk: single location in a small, landlocked market with limited fresh fish supply
Key-person risk: Sam's reputation and quality may be tied closely to the owner/chef
Limited growth: only two menu items constrains revenue upside; closed one day per week caps capacity
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on lease terms, supplier contracts, and chef retention
Assess whether the Michelin distinction and competitive moat are durable without the current owner
Explore whether Sam's could expand (additional location, catering) to justify the $2M price
